title: Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relations in Chaotic Andreev Billiards
authors: I. R. A. C. Lucena, T. J. A. Mori, M. M. Soares, D. Bazeia, A. R. Rocha
abstract: We investigate how particle-hole symmetry, quantum interference, and tunnel barriers shape thermodynamic uncertainty relations in chaotic Andreev billiards. Using random-matrix theory and the Mahaux-Weidenmüller scattering approach, we study charge conductance and shot noise across the four Altland-Zirnbauer symmetry classes, from the single-channel extreme quantum limit to the multichannel semiclassical regime and from ideal to opaque contacts. We characterize thermodynamic precision through two complementary ensemble observables: either by averaging the sample-resolved noise-to-conductance ratio, or from the separately averaging noise and conductance. Their pronounced discrepancy in the extreme quantum regime reveals the non-self-averaging character of mesoscopic transport and persists over a broad range of barrier transparencies. For ideal contacts, the first provides a sensitive fingerprint of the Altland-Zirnbauer symmetry class. In the opaque regime, this hierarchy changes. Despite these strong symmetry- and barrier-dependent effects, the standard thermodynamic uncertainty relation remains satisfied throughout all regimes investigated. Our results establish thermodynamic uncertainty as a symmetry-sensitive probe of universal transport in chaotic normal-superconducting systems.
summary: This work analyzes the Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relations in chaotic Andreev billiards, a system exhibiting particle-hole symmetry. By using RMT, the authors test how quantum interference and barrier transparency affect the TUR across various symmetry classes. They confirm that the fundamental thermodynamic bound remains satisfied, establishing TUR as a powerful symmetry-sensitive diagnostic tool for superconducting quantum transport.
main_problem: The study investigates how particle-hole symmetry, quantum interference, and tunnel barriers influence the Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relations (TUR) in chaotic Andreev billiards.
main_result: The standard TUR bound is consistently satisfied across all investigated regimes, confirming that Andreev billiards remain compatible with fundamental thermodynamic constraints.
method: The research employs Random Matrix Theory (RMT) and the Mahaux–Weidenmüller scattering approach to analyze transport properties.
model_or_system: The system is an open chaotic Andreev billiard, modeled using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) Hamiltonian, which inherently possesses particle-hole symmetry.
key_observables: Charge conductance, shot noise power, and the TUR observable, $Q$, which is compared using two ensemble averages ($Q_R$ and $Q_{MS}$).
important_parameters: The analysis spans multiple regimes: the extreme quantum limit ($N=1$) to the semiclassical multichannel regime ($N=10$), and varying barrier transparencies ($\Gamma$) from ideal to opaque.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Random Matrix Theory framework and assumes operation within the universal RMT regime ($	au_\phi, 	au_D \gg 	au_E$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of conductance, noise, and the TUR observable on barrier transparency ($\Gamma$) for different symmetry classes and system sizes, showing the relative contributions of quantum interference.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the TUR across different symmetry classes and transport regimes, comparing two distinct definitions of the TUR observable to probe mesoscopic fluctuations and the role of quantum interference corrections.
why_interesting: The investigation of TUR in superconducting mesoscopic systems provides a unique, symmetry-sensitive probe of universal transport, linking quantum chaos, superconductivity, and fundamental thermodynamic laws.

The mesoscopic cavity is coupled to two normal-metal electron reservoirs at chemical potentials µ1 and µ2 via leads supporting N1 and N2 open channels, and to superconducting contacts, S1 and S2. In the ballistic regime, electrons undergo multiple coherent reflections, leading to chaotic scattering.
